data:
Claimward separates a control plane, the server, from the data plane, the WireGuard tunnel between a device and the gateway. Authentication is delegated to your identity provider: Claimward never sees a password.
On a device, an unprivileged app signs the person in and keeps the session; a privileged helper (root, or SYSTEM on Windows) enrolls with the server and owns the tunnel. The app never talks to the server itself.
data.end-to-end-enrollment-flow#End-to-end en: ┌──────────┐ 1. sign-in: GitHub device flow, OIDC code + PKCE, ┌──────────┐ │ app │ or go-authn device flow (+ key registration) │ IdP │ │ (as you) │◀─────────────────── bearer token ──────────────────│ │ └────┬─────┘ └──────────┘ │ 2. socket: connect {server_url, bearer, private key, tenant} ▼ ┌──────────┐ 3. POST /api/v1/enroll ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ helper │ Authorization: Bearer │ claimward-vpn-server │ │ (root) │ {public_key, device, tenant} ───▶ │ verify the bearer │ │ │ │ choose the tenant │ │ │ ◀─── 4. {assigned_ip, │ allocate an address │ │ │ server_public_key, endpoint, │ wgctrl: add the peer │ │ │ allowed_ips, dns, │ (AllowedIPs = ip/32) │ │ │ grpc_endpoint, keepalive, └───────────┬─────────────┘ │ │ lease_expires_at} │ RouteService │ │ ◀═════════════ 6. gRPC Watch (TLS) ═══════════════╛ (live routes) │ │ │ │ 5. wireguard-go: utunN / Wintun "Claimward", address, routes └────┬─────┘ ╚═══════════════════ WireGuard tunnel ════════════════════▶ private network The app signs the person in with the configured provider: GitHub by default (OAuth device flow), any OpenID Connect issuer (authorization code with PKCE, in the browser), or a go-authn provider (device flow). The bearer it gets is a GitHub access token, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token. With go-authn, the device’s public key is first registered at the provider, and the bearer is the token that registration returns. The app generates the device’s WireGuard key pair at the first sign-in and keeps it in its encrypted session file (session.enc, whose key is in the Keychain or the Secret Service; session.dpapi on Windows) until the person signs out, so the device keeps its public key across connections (and its address while it is enrolled). To connect, it hands the helper the server URL, the bearer, the private key and the tenant chosen for the session, over the helper’s socket. The helper checks that the server is one its own configuration names, then calls POST /api/v1/enroll with the device’s public key and the bearer. The server verifies the bearer (a GitHub API call, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token whose subject must own the key), applies any organisation or email-domain allowlist, picks the tenant, allocates a VPN address and programs the gateway (wgctrl) with a peer whose only allowed IP is that /32. It answers with the tunnel parameters: the address, its own public key, the endpoint, the tenant’s routes and DNS servers, the keepalive, the RouteService endpoint and the lease’s end. The helper brings up a userspace tunnel with wireguard-go, gives the interface its address and installs the routes. When the server advertises a RouteService (GRPC_ENDPOINT), the helper watches it over gRPC: route changes made to the tenant reach the device without enrolling again.
data.leases#Leases:
Each enrollment carries a lease of LEASE_TTL (24 hours by default). A background reaper on the server removes, every minute, the peers whose lease has ended, so a lost or revoked device falls off the gateway on its own. With go-authn a lease never outlives the key’s registration at the provider.
The server renews a lease on POST /api/v1/heartbeat, and removes a peer at once on POST /api/v1/deregister.
From claimward-vpn-client v0.3.1, that is from the app releases that carry it (the macOS, Linux and Windows apps from v0.2.0), the helper keeps the lease itself while the tunnel is up. It renews at half of what the lease has left, never sooner than 30 seconds nor later than 10 minutes, and acts on the answer:
The server answers The helper a renewed lease renews again at half of it 404 not_enrolled: it forgot the device (the lease ran out, or the server restarted) enrolls again with the same key and tenant, and brings the tunnel up from that answer; if that fails too, takes the tunnel down 403 (not_a_member, key_not_registered): access withdrawn takes the tunnel down, and reports why (last_error) 401, a 5xx, or nothing retries within a minute, sooner than the lease ends The helper renews with the last bearer it was given. That is enough for a GitHub token, not for a go-authn access token, which expires in minutes and which only the app can refresh. So while the app runs, pkg/appcore hands the helper a fresh bearer (the helper’s renew action) at 40% of what the lease has left (at most 8 minutes apart), before the helper’s own renewal is due. An app restarted under a running tunnel starts doing so at its first status poll.
Disconnect (the helper’s down) deregisters the peer, giving its address back at once. A helper that is stopping (its service manager stops it, or the machine shuts down) takes the tunnel down without deregistering, so a helper restarted finds the lease still there, and a stopped machine’s lease runs out on the server.
The v0.1.0 apps are built on earlier client versions, which do none of this: they renew a lease only by connecting again, and leave the peer on the gateway after Disconnect until its lease ends.
data.trust-boundaries#Trust boundaries: The server is the only component that talks to the identity provider to verify a sign-in, and the only one with rights to change the gateway’s peers. On the device, the helper is the only privileged process. Anything that can reach its socket can ask it to act, so it acts within its own configuration: it enrolls only with the servers that configuration names and takes no tunnel configuration from a request. See Privileged helper. The app runs as the person. It holds the session (bearer token and device key) in an encrypted file, never in clear on disk: sealed with a key kept in the macOS Keychain or the Linux Secret Service, or with Windows DPAPI. With no usable store, sign-in fails. A route watch carries the bearer token, so it runs over TLS except to a loopback address. The wire contract lives in one place, claimward-vpn-client/pkg/protocol and pkg/routespb, imported by both the clients and the server.

data: Serverclaimward-vpn-server v0.10.0: the control plane on the gateway host. Client libraryclaimward-vpn-client v0.7.0: what the apps and the server share. Privileged helperThe root or SYSTEM process that enrolls and owns the tunnel. macOS appclaimward-vpn-app-osx v0.8.0: native window and status item, go-widgets. Linux appclaimward-vpn-app-linux v0.7.0: window and tray in pure Go, systemd helper. Windows appclaimward-vpn-app-windows v0.8.0: window and tray in pure Go, helper service, Wintun.

claimward-vpn-client v0.12.0 is a Go library. It ships no binary: the runnable programs are the apps’ (cmd/claimward-app and cmd/claimward-helper in each app repository). The server imports it too, for the wire types and the gRPC stubs.
There is no claimward command-line client. Earlier versions of this module had one (cmd/claimward, with login and connect); it was removed, and the library-only module is what the apps build on.
data.files-on-the-device#Files on the device:
File What /Claimward/config.json the app’s configuration (appcore.Config), 0600, its socket may be overridden by CLAIMWARD_HELPER_SOCKET /claimward/session.enc (macOS and Linux), session.dpapi (Windows) the sealed session; its key is in the Keychain (macOS) or the Secret Service (Linux), or the blob is DPAPI-protected. On Linux the blob is sealed with AES-GCM and only its key is in the Secret Service. is Go’s os.UserConfigDir(): ~/Library/Application Support on macOS, ~/.config on Linux, %AppData% on Windows.
This is the format of client v0.10.0 and later, which connects to several servers at once. The person types only a server URL; the name, providers, exclusivity and logo are read from the server’s /.well-known/claimward-configuration.
{ "version": 2, "servers": [ {"url": "https://vpn.example.com", "provider": "campus"}, {"url": "https://lab.example.org"} ], "socket_path": "/var/run/claimward-helper.sock" } config.json key version 2 servers[].url the server’s base URL (https://; http:// only for loopback); must be one the helper is configured for servers[].provider optional: the id of the provider chosen from the server’s document socket_path optional: the helper’s socket, if not the default. May be overridden by CLAIMWARD_HELPER_SOCKET, the only variable left A file of v0.9.0 or earlier (server_url, provider, github_client_id, oidc_issuer, oidc_client_id, and the CLAIMWARD_SERVER, CLAIMWARD_AUTH_PROVIDER, CLAIMWARD_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, CLAIMWARD_OIDC_* variables) is migrated once on first load. An exclusive server is refused while any other is connected, and any other is refused while an exclusive one is; the refusal names the blocking server. Since v0.11.0 every platform holds one tunnel per server, each on its own deterministic interface (below).
Since v0.11.0 the helper’s servers is optional (the administrator’s pre-approval) and a server the person adds is trusted only once the system has consented: see Server approval. The helper’s helper.json gains approvals, the file of approved servers.
data.packages#Packages: Package Purpose pkg/protocol the wire contract (/enroll, /tenants, /heartbeat, /deregister), shared with the server pkg/routespb generated gRPC/protobuf stubs of the RouteService, shared with the server pkg/auth interactive sign-in behind a Provider: GitHub device flow (default), OIDC code + PKCE, or go-authn device flow, whose provider also registers the device’s key (KeyRegistrar) pkg/oidc the OIDC authorization code + PKCE flow: discovery, loopback redirect pkg/browser opens a URL in the default browser with absolute opener paths, so it works from GUI apps pkg/client Enroll, Tenants, Heartbeat, Deregister against the server, and TunnelConfig to turn an EnrollResponse into a wgtun.Config pkg/wgkey WireGuard key generation and parsing pkg/pathmtu fits the tunnel MTU to the path: the server’s mtu (default 1420), lowered to the interface MTU towards the endpoint minus 60 (IPv4) or 80 (IPv6), never below 1280, never above the server’s value; standard library only pkg/wgtun userspace WireGuard tunnel with wireguard-go, plus address and routes: ifconfig/route on macOS, ip on Linux, a Wintun adapter through winipcfg on Windows (with DNS and MTU); needs privileges pkg/routeclient watches the server’s RouteService and reports route updates; TLS except to loopback pkg/appcore the apps’ logic, shared by the three: sign-in, the tenant chosen for the session, connect and disconnect through the helper, status for the UI pkg/appvm the apps’ view model, with no UI in it: the screen to show, what each command may do, the status poll, the events (tunnel dropped, session expired) and, since v0.12.0, each tunnel’s facts (State.Tunnel: interface, address, endpoint, allowed IPs, DNS, MTU, bytes received and sent, last handshake); each app adapts it to its own widgets pkg/helper the privileged helper, shared by the three apps: enrolls, owns the tunnel, watches route pushes, and approves servers with the system’s consent (Server approval) pkg/hproto, pkg/helperclient the helper’s socket protocol, and the app’s client for it: Approve, ApproveElevated, Revoke, Approved, and the typed errors *NotApprovedError and ErrApprovalDenied pkg/macauth macOS Authorization Services for server approval: Obtain(prompt) in the app, Verify in the helper pkg/tokenstore the session (bearer, refresh token, device private key, chosen tenant) in the OS secret store: macOS Keychain, Windows DPAPI, Linux Secret Service; no plaintext fallback
data.platform-notes#Platform notes: DNS. The server’s DNS servers are applied on Windows only; on macOS and Linux they are carried in the protocol but pkg/wgtun does not apply them yet. Route pushes replace the allowed IPs and the routes; DNS changes in a push are not applied. Interface names. One interface per server, named from the server’s URL by wgtun.InterfaceName: macOS utunN (numbered by the kernel), Linux cw- and ten hex digits of the URL’s SHA-256 (13 bytes, within the 15 of IFNAMSIZ), Windows Claimward <6 hex>. Reconnecting replaces the interface; a leftover of that name is removed first, and a Linux TUN device goes with its process, so a crashed helper leaves none. Windows. The device is a Wintun adapter, one per server (see above): wintun.dll (from https://www.wintun.net, signed by WireGuard LLC) must sit beside the executable that calls wgtun.Up, which the Windows app’s packaging takes care of. Address, routes, DNS and MTU are set through winipcfg (the IP Helper API, pure Go, CGO_ENABLED=0). Session store. The platform’s secret store: the macOS login Keychain (holding an AES-GCM key; the session is sealed in session.enc), Windows DPAPI (session.dpapi), and on Linux a sealed session.enc too, whose AES-GCM key is kept in the Secret Service through secret-tool. Since v0.5.0 there is no plaintext fallback and CLAIMWARD_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT_SESSION has no effect: with no usable store, saving the session fails and sign-in fails with an error naming what is missing (on Linux, install and unlock a Secret Service provider such as gnome-keyring or KeePassXC, and secret-tool). A legacy session.json is read once, moved into the store and deleted, or deleted if the store refuses it. Tests of other packages use tokenstore.UseMemory().
data.use-in-your-own-tooling#Use in your own: ctx := context.Background() // 1. Sign in. GitHub is the default provider (device flow). provider, err := auth.New(auth.Config{Provider: "github", GitHubClientID: "Iv1.0123456789abcdef"}) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } tok, err := provider.Login(ctx, func(p auth.DevicePrompt) { fmt.Printf("visit %s and enter code %s\n", p.VerificationURI, p.UserCode) }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } // 2. A key pair, and with go-authn the PUBLIC key registered first: the // token for the server is the one RegisterKey returns. keys, err := wgkey.Generate() if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } if reg, ok := provider.(auth.KeyRegistrar); ok { if tok, err = reg.RegisterKey(ctx, tok, keys.Public.String(), "laptop"); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // 3. Enroll; "" lets the server use the person's only tenant. c := client.New("https://vpn.example.com") resp, err := c.Enroll(ctx, tok.Value, keys.Public, protocol.DeviceInfo{Name: "laptop", OS: "linux", Platform: "my-tool"}, "") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } // 4. The tunnel (needs privileges), and optionally live routes. cfg, err := client.TunnelConfig(resp, keys.Private) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } tun, err := wgtun.Up(cfg) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } defer tun.Close() if resp.GRPCEndpoint != "" { go routeclient.Watch(ctx, resp.GRPCEndpoint, tok.Value, keys.Public.String(), func(u routeclient.Update) { _ = tun.UpdateRoutes(u.AllowedIPs) }) } A long-lived client renews its lease with c.Heartbeat before resp.LeaseExpiresAt, and removes its peer with c.Deregister when it is done.

data:
Each app has a privileged helper: a root LaunchDaemon on macOS, a systemd service on Linux, the ClaimwardHelper service (LocalSystem) on Windows. It is the only privileged process of the app. All three are the same code, pkg/helper of claimward-vpn-client; each app supplies only a main that loads the configuration and listens.
The helper does the server communication as well as the tunnel: it enrolls, brings the tunnel up, and watches route pushes. On macOS “Local Network” privacy blocks an unprivileged app from a server on the LAN and root is exempt; the other platforms follow the same path so that the three apps behave alike.
data.bounded-by-its-own-configuration#Bounded:
Any process that can reach the helper’s socket can make it act, so what it does is bounded by its own configuration, never by the request:
It enrolls only with a server its configuration names, or one that was approved with the system’s consent. A helper that took the server from the request would let any local process point it at a server of its own, answering with routes for 0.0.0.0/0: every packet of the machine, sent where that process chose. Approval is the operating system’s own prompt (macOS Authorization Services, polkit on Linux, an elevated second socket on Windows), never a field of the request: see Server approval. It takes no tunnel configuration from a request. The tunnel is what that server answered at enrollment. The earlier up and update-routes actions, which took one, are gone. Its configuration must be root’s (SYSTEM’s or the Administrators’ on Windows) and writable by nobody else, or the helper does not start: whoever writes it chooses the servers trusted. { "servers": ["https://vpn.example.org"], "group": "claimward", "socket": "/var/run/claimward-helper.sock" } Key servers optional since v0.11.0: the servers pre-approved by the administrator (compared without a trailing /); others need approval approvals optional: where the approved servers are kept (the default per platform is in Server approval) group who may use the socket beside root: admin on macOS, claimward on Linux, Claimward Users on Windows by default socket /var/run/claimward-helper.sock by default, C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.sock on Windows Platform helper.json macOS /Library/Application Support/Claimward/helper.json Linux /etc/claimward/helper.json Windows C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.json
data.packaging-the-polkit-policy-linux#Packag: The Linux package installs packaging/polkit/com.claimward.helper.approve-server.policy of the client repository into /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/. Without it polkit does not know the action and every approval is refused.
data.route-watches-over-tls#Route watches ove:
A route watch carries the bearer token, so pkg/routeclient runs it over TLS, checked against the system’s roots, except to a loopback address. Against a server whose RouteService is not TLS the handshake fails before the token is sent, and the tunnel stays up without live route updates.
Stopping the helper takes the tunnel down.
data.the-socket-macos-and-linux#The socket: m: The socket is 0660, owned by root and the helper’s group. It is created with a restrictive umask, so it never exists with a wider mode, in a directory only root can write (the helper refuses one somebody else could, since they could replace the socket with their own and receive the app’s bearer). The earlier helper’s socket was 0666.
data.the-socket-protocol#The socket protocol:
One JSON request per connection, one JSON response (pkg/hproto):
Action What the helper does connect enrolls with the server named in the request, if its configuration allows it, with the bearer, private key, device name and tenant given; brings the tunnel up; watches the RouteService tenants asks the server which tenants the bearer may connect to down takes the tunnel down: the named server’s, or, with no server, the caller’s own (see Whose tunnels) status for each of the caller’s tunnels: the interface, the address, the tenant and, since v0.12.0, its live facts (see below) approve since v0.11.0: approves the server named in the request, if the operating system consents (see Server approval) revoke removes a server from the approved ones approved lists the approved servers Since v0.11.0 the helper holds one tunnel per server, each on its own interface, named from the server’s URL: on Windows the adapter is no longer called Claimward but Claimward <6 hex> (a breaking change for anything that looked the adapter up by its old name).
data.the-socket-windows#The socket: Windows:
On Windows the same rules are ACLs, which the helper sets and reads back itself rather than trusting an installer to have done it:
the socket’s directory, C:\ProgramData\Claimward, gets a protected DACL (nothing inherited from ProgramData, which lets every user create files there): SYSTEM and Administrators in full control, the socket’s group allowed to list and traverse it and nothing more. It is created already carrying that DACL, and a directory that is a junction or a link is refused; the socket gets its own DACL: SYSTEM, Administrators, and the group allowed to connect (read/write); the group is the local group Claimward Users, which the installer creates. If it does not exist the socket is opened to INTERACTIVE (everybody logged on at the machine, console or Remote Desktop) and the helper logs that it did; helper.json must be owned by SYSTEM or Administrators, and writable by nobody else: the helper reads the file’s owner and DACL and refuses any allow entry that grants write, append, delete, WRITE_DAC, WRITE_OWNER or generic write/all to another SID, and a null DACL. The rules (pkg/helper/acl.go) are pure functions, tested on every platform; the Windows CI job applies them to real files and reads them back.
Approval has a second socket on Windows, C:\ProgramData\Claimward\approve.sock (helper.ListenElevated, served by Server.ServeElevated), whose ACL names SYSTEM and Administrators only: a standard user cannot connect without UAC elevation, and only an approve that arrived there counts. The app reaches it through Client.ElevatedSocketPath and ApproveElevated.
data.what-status-reports-per-tunnel#What stat:
Since v0.12.0 each tunnel in the answer carries, read-only, what a detail panel shows (the fields are omitted when empty):
Field Meaning interface, assigned_ip the interface name and the address, apart from each other endpoint the peer’s host:port, as the device holds it now allowed_ips the CIDRs routed into the tunnel (they follow a route push) dns, mtu the DNS servers the server assigned, and the interface’s MTU rx_bytes, tx_bytes bytes the device received from and sent to the peer since the tunnel came up last_handshake the last completed handshake (absent until there has been one) The live values are read from the WireGuard device itself (the cross-platform UAPI get operation), so a roaming endpoint or a new route shows at once; if the device cannot be read, the enrollment’s values are reported and the counters stay at zero. The answer never contains a key or a bearer. Since v0.12.1 status lists only the tunnels the caller owns (next section). The apps poll it, once a second while a detail panel is open.
data.whose-tunnels#Whose tunnels:
Since v0.12.1 a tunnel belongs to the user who connected it, and status (with its last_errors) shows a caller only its own tunnels. On a shared machine one user no longer sees another’s endpoint, routes, address or counters.
The owner is read from the kernel, never from the request. At connect the helper asks the operating system who is on the other end of that connection: the uid (SO_PEERCRED on Linux, LOCAL_PEERCRED on macOS and FreeBSD), or on Windows the user SID of the token of the connecting process. No field of a request can name an owner. root sees and does everything, and so do SYSTEM, an elevated Administrator and any caller of the elevated socket on Windows. Acting on another user’s tunnel is refused: down of a named server, renew, revoke, and a connect that would replace it answer with the error_code tunnel_not_owned. down with no server takes down the caller’s own tunnels. A refused connect asks the server nothing. A caller the system cannot identify is refused (since v0.12.2; v0.12.1 pooled such callers). Every action, connect, down and status included, answers with the error_code caller_not_identified: the helper fails closed. It happens on a Windows that does not answer the peer-process question, and on a platform with no peer-credential call. Limit: an exclusive connect that is refused because another tunnel holds the machine still names that server (blocked_by), as exclusivity is machine-wide. The wire format is unchanged: no field was added, so apps built against v0.12.0 work as they are.

data: claimward-vpn-app-linux v0.7.0 is a window and a tray icon drawn in pure Go with go-widgets: no webview, no cgo (CGO_ENABLED=0). The four settings text fields are native GTK 4 entries (system input methods, selection, clipboard), loaded at run time without cgo; the desktop entry starts the app with GO_WIDGETS_GTK=1. Without libgtk-4 the app falls back to painted fields. The native fields show no placeholder text. A privileged helper run by systemd owns the WireGuard tunnel. The logic is the macOS app’s: both use pkg/appcore and pkg/helper.
data.configure#Configure:
The app: ~/.config/Claimward/config.json, written by the settings form, mode 0600, overridden by CLAIMWARD_* variables (see the client library). The session (tokens and the device’s WireGuard key) is sealed with AES-GCM in session.enc; the key is kept in the desktop’s Secret Service keyring through secret-tool. It is never written to disk in clear. A Secret Service provider is required (client v0.5.0 and later): install and unlock one such as gnome-keyring or KeePassXC, and install secret-tool (libsecret-tools). Without one, sign-in fails with an error naming what is missing; there is no plaintext fallback, on a headless server either. A session.json left by an older version is moved into the keyring on first start, or deleted if the keyring refuses it.
The tunnel MTU is the server’s mtu, lowered to fit the path to the server (the interface MTU towards its endpoint, minus 60 for IPv4 or 80 for IPv6) and never below 1280 (client v0.6.0, pkg/pathmtu).
The helper: /etc/claimward/helper.json (see Privileged helper); after editing it, sudo systemctl restart claimward-helper.
data.design#Design: claimward-app (your session) ├─ internal/view go-widgets/toolkit widgets, bound with go-widgets/mvvmtk ├─ internal/trayview tray icon + menu (StatusNotifierItem over D-Bus) ├─ internal/viewmodel all state as go-widgets/mvvm observables and commands └─ appcore sign-in, tenant, session; drives the helper │ X11 / Wayland │ unix socket, JSON, 0660 root:claimward ▼ ▼ the window, the tray claimward-helper (root, systemd) enrolls with a configured server, wireguard-go TUN + ip(8), route pushes The app runs as you and never touches the network configuration or the server itself: everything goes through the helper. The view model holds every piece of state and imports no widget; CI enforces MVVM with mvvmlint and “no hand-drawn UI” with bricolint.
data.install#Install:
Build as yourself (Go 1.27.4 or later), then install as root:
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o bin/ ./cmd/... sudo ./scripts/install.sh --server https://vpn.example.com --server accepts https URLs only: the sign-in token is sent to that server, so a plain http:// URL is refused.
install.sh:
creates the claimward group and adds you to it ($SUDO_USER, or --user): log out and back in for it to apply; installs claimward-app to /usr/local/bin and claimward-helper to /usr/local/sbin (--prefix to change); writes /etc/claimward/helper.json, root:root, mode 0644, with the server given (an existing file is kept); installs and starts claimward-helper.service, and waits for its socket; installs the desktop entry and the icon. Start Claimward VPN from the desktop’s menu; claimward-app -hidden starts in the tray (for an autostart entry). sudo ./scripts/uninstall.sh removes it all and stops the helper, which takes the tunnel down; --purge also removes /etc/claimward and the group.
data.the-hardened-unit#The hardened unit:
claimward-helper.service keeps only CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW and CAP_CHOWN, with NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict and only /run writable, ProtectHome, /dev/net/tun alone from /dev, address families limited to unix, inet, inet6 and netlink, and the @system-service system calls. systemd-analyze security claimward-helper rates it 2.5 (OK). Being in the claimward group means being allowed to bring the VPN up and down.
Verified in an Ubuntu 24.04 (arm64) virtual machine against a stand-in server. Not yet verified, according to the README: a real GNOME or KDE desktop, Wayland, HiDPI, a sign-in against a real identity provider, and a real claimward-vpn-server.
data.what-it-does#What it does: Status: who is signed in, connected or not, the address and interface, the session’s tenant, whether the helper answers, the server. It is polled every 2 seconds. The screens, what each button may do and the poll are the shared pkg/appvm of the client (v0.7.0), which the app’s view model only adapts to observables. Notifications: when the tunnel drops, or the session expires, the app sends a desktop notification, once per change; clicking it opens the window. Your own Disconnect and Sign out are not announced, and a notification that cannot be sent is logged and changes nothing. Sign in: for a device flow the window shows the code and an Open sign-in page button (xdg-open); the sign-in can be cancelled. Tenant: when the server refuses a connection because the person belongs to several, the window says so and offers a drop-down; Choose tenant asks for the list ahead of time. The tenant cannot be changed while connected. Connect / Disconnect / Sign out, Settings (server URL, provider, GitHub client ID, OIDC issuer and client ID), and the connection log. Tray: a status line, Connect, Disconnect, Open window, Quit; the icon is in colour while connected. Closing the window leaves the app in the tray; Quit leaves the tunnel as it is. The tray needs a StatusNotifierItem host (KDE Plasma, GNOME with the AppIndicator and KStatusNotifierItem Support extension, waybar…). Without one, or if the tray item cannot be put on the session bus, the app says so on start-up and closing the window quits it.

data: claimward-vpn-app-osx v0.11.0 is a native app written in Go: one window and a menu-bar status item, drawn by go-widgets, with the system’s own NSTextField and NSPopUpButton for the inputs. There is no webview, no local web server and no JavaScript (before v0.7.0 the window was a Svelte page in a webview). Its logic (sign-in, tenant choice, connect) and its helper are the shared pkg/appcore and pkg/helper; the view model is pkg/appvm, the same one the Linux and Windows apps use.
data.build#Build:
With go-task:
task config:init # a starter config.json (local Dex) task install-helper SERVER=https://vpn.example.org # build and install the helper (sudo) task start:bundle # build Claimward.app and open it Run the bundle rather than the bare binary: notifications are refused to a process that is not in an app bundle, so from a bare binary a dropped tunnel only reaches the log. By hand (no Node toolchain any more):
CGO_ENABLED=1 go build -o bin/claimward-app ./cmd/claimward-app CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o bin/claimward-helper ./cmd/claimward-helper
data.configure#Configure:
Nothing has to be written by hand: + adds a server by its URL. The app keeps the list in ~/Library/Application Support/Claimward/config.json (app v0.10.0 and later, client v0.11.0; the format is described on the client page):
{ "version": 2, "servers": [ {"url": "https://vpn.example.com"} ] } Only the server URL is configured; the providers come from the server. With GitHub and go-authn, clicking Connect shows a code to enter at the displayed page; with OIDC the browser opens the provider’s sign-in page. Older builds (client v0.9.0 and earlier) read server_url, provider, github_client_id, oidc_issuer and oidc_client_id instead; a file in that format is migrated once, on first start, and its session is adopted by the matching server.
data.design#Design:
claimward-app (one process, as you) ├─ window go-widgets, with NSTextField / NSPopUpButton embedded ├─ status item NSStatusItem: status / Open Claimward… / Connect / Disconnect / Quit ├─ notifications when the tunnel drops or the session expires (from the app bundle) └─ view model pkg/appvm over appcore: sign-in, tenant choice, session │ Unix socket (JSON), 0660 root:admin ▼ claimward-helper (root LaunchDaemon) enrolls with the server, wireguard-go: utunN, route pushes The app is one unprivileged process that owns all state. The text input (the server URL) is the system’s text field, with its input method and spell checking; the provider and tenant choices are pop-up buttons. The helper enrolls with the server and owns the tunnel. Closing the window hides it: the app keeps running in the status item and quits through its Quit item.
The window opens at 800 x 480 points (the size of WireGuard’s macOS manager). The Servers sidebar on the left lists the servers, each with its logo (a neutral mark when it has none), its name and its state; +, − and a gear are under the list. Several servers may be connected at once, and each row shows its own state.
The detail panel on the right is a key/value table with section titles, in the manner of WireGuard’s tunnel panel. It hides every empty field except Status and refreshes every second. Server holds the name and logo, the URL, the identity provider and the signed-in identity, the tenant, whether the server is exclusive, and whether the helper has approved it. Status has an icon and the Connect / Disconnect buttons. Interface holds the status, the address, the DNS servers, the MTU and the lease expiry in relative time. Peer holds the endpoint, the allowed IPs, the latest handshake as “12 s ago” and the transfer as “3.50 MiB received, 900 B sent” (needs client v0.12.0); each section is hidden while it is empty. Edit is at the bottom right. When the server lists several identity providers, sign-in shows one button per provider.
Every button carries a Tabler icon (go-widgets/tabler-icons, MIT), and the servers’ logos are drawn by the toolkit’s SVG logo widget. Unlike WireGuard’s rows, which truncate, any text wider than its box wraps: URLs, identities, routes, refusal reasons and the connection log. Rows grow to hold their lines, and the detail panel scrolls when it is taller than the 800 x 480 window, so nothing is clipped.
+ opens a window of its own with only a URL field. Next asks the server for its public discovery document and previews its name, logo, providers and whether it is exclusive; the person confirms before the server is added, and a server that does not answer as a Claimward server is told in plain words. The gear (or Edit) opens the same window on the selected server, prefilled, and can change its identity provider; it is disabled, with the reason in its accessible label, while no server is selected.
Connect on a server the helper has not approved asks macOS for an administrator’s authorization, naming the server’s host, then approves the server and connects (see server approval). A refusal is shown as such. − offers to revoke the approval with the removal. An exclusive server, or a connection that blocks the others, disables Connect and says why, for instance “Alpha is connected and exclusive”.
data.install-the-helper-and-run#Install the h: sudo ./scripts/install-helper.sh https://vpn.example.org # more servers may follow open dist/Claimward.app # then click Connect The installer copies the helper to /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/, writes /Library/Application Support/Claimward/helper.json (root’s, mode 0644) with the servers given, and loads the LaunchDaemon com.claimward.helper. The helper’s socket is /var/run/claimward-helper.sock, 0660, root:admin; it logs to /var/log/claimward-helper.log. sudo ./scripts/uninstall-helper.sh removes it.
data.release#Release:
.github/workflows/release.yml builds Claimward.dmg on v* tags and attaches it to the release. When the signing secrets are set it signs the app with a Developer ID and notarizes and staples the DMG; without them it falls back to an ad-hoc signature, which Gatekeeper blocks on a downloaded DMG. The repository holds no signing secrets, so the published DMGs (v0.1.0 and v0.2.0) are ad-hoc signed and not notarized. The DMG holds the app (with the helper binary inside it); the helper is installed as above.
Still to come: the helper installed with SMJobBless, a release signed with a Developer ID, and DNS applied on macOS.
data.session-and-servers#Session and servers:
The session (tokens and the device’s WireGuard key) lives in session.enc, sealed with AES-GCM; the key is held in the login Keychain. It is never written to disk in clear and there is no plaintext fallback: if the Keychain is locked or unavailable (client v0.5.0 and later), sign-in fails with an error saying so. A 0600 session.json from an older version is moved into the store on first start, or deleted if that fails.
The tunnel MTU is the server’s mtu, lowered to fit the path to the server (the interface MTU towards its endpoint, minus 60 for IPv4 or 80 for IPv6) and never below 1280 (client v0.6.0, pkg/pathmtu).
The server must be an https URL. Since v0.7.0 there is no loopback UI API and no launch token: the window and the logic share one process.
data.tenants#Tenants: A person in several tenants chooses one in the detail panel’s Tenant pop-up, which lists them once the server has offered them; Refresh asks again. The choice holds for the session; a new sign-in forgets it. A Connect from the menu bar that the server refuses for want of a choice opens the window.

data: claimward-vpn-server v0.14.0 is the control plane. It verifies the bearer a device presents, allocates VPN addresses, and programs the WireGuard gateway with one peer per enrolled device. It runs on the gateway host, beside an existing wg0: Linux (nftables) or, from v0.10.0, OpenBSD (pf, see OpenBSD).
data.configuration#Configuration:
Settings are in the environment. Secrets are not: since v0.6.0 they are files in a credentials directory, see Credentials below.
Variable Required Default Notes PROVIDERS_FILE ✅ — JSON file listing the identity providers (since v0.14.0, breaking), see Identity providers. It replaces AUTH_PROVIDER, OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID: the server refuses to start while one of them is set GITHUB_API_URL https://api.github.com the API the tenants’ named members are resolved against; set for GitHub Enterprise. Each github provider has its own api_url in the providers file SERVER_LOGO_FILE — an SVG logo published in the discovery document and at /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg (since v0.14.0); at most 64 KiB, validated at start (no script, no external reference): an invalid file refuses to start GOAUTHN_PEER_LIST_INTERVAL 30s how often the list of registered keys is fetched GOAUTHN_SSF false also poll the provider’s Shared Signals stream, so that a disabling is acted on at once; the gateway’s client must be an SSF receiver there GOAUTHN_SSF_INTERVAL 5s how often the SSF stream is polled WG_ENDPOINT ✅ — public host:port of the gateway, advertised to clients CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY ✅ — the directory that holds the secret files, see Credentials WG_INTERFACE wg0 interface to manage WG_DRYRUN false log peer operations instead of applying them (local development) VPN_CIDR 10.80.0.0/24 IPv4 address pool; its first host is the gateway’s PUSH_ROUTES VPN_CIDR CSV routes of the default tenant DNS — CSV DNS servers of the default tenant TENANTS_FILE — JSON file of tenants loaded at start, with their access policy KEEPALIVE 25 persistent keepalive advertised to clients (seconds) LEASE_TTL 24h how long an enrollment lasts without a heartbeat TUNNEL_MTU derived MTU of the WireGuard interface, 1280 to 9000, advertised as mtu; anything else refuses to start. Unset: the uplink MTU minus 80, at most 1420, at least 1280. The same atomic inet claimward table also clamps the MSS of every TCP SYN crossing the interface (forwarded both ways, and input for the gateway itself) to this MTU minus 40 (IPv4) or 60 (IPv6) LISTEN_ADDR :8443 HTTP listen address GRPC_ADDR :8444 RouteService listen address; Watch streams are re-authorised every 15 s and end when the identity is no longer allowed METRICS_ADDR — (off) separate listener for /metrics, served only when set (since v0.9.0 there is no default port: the old 127.0.0.1:9090 clashed with Prometheus); never on LISTEN_ADDR. It names every tenant: keep it on loopback or a private network MAX_DEVICES_PER_SUBJECT 5 devices one identity may enroll SERVER_NAME — display name published in the discovery document (since v0.13.0); at most 100 characters, no control characters; unset, none is published SERVER_EXCLUSIVE false published in the discovery document (since v0.13.0): this server refuses to share the machine with other Claimward tunnels; clients refuse to connect it alongside others, and refuse others while it is connected. true or false, anything else refuses to start GRPC_ENDPOINT — host:port of the RouteService advertised to clients; empty, they do not watch TLS_CERT / TLS_KEY — HTTPS, and TLS on the RouteService DEBUG — any value: debug logging (one line per request)
data.credentials#Credentials:
Every secret is a file in the directory named by CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, never an environment variable: an environment is copied into every child process and every crash dump. systemd sets the variable for LoadCredential= and LoadCredentialEncrypted=; on the other platforms you set it yourself. The file names are fixed, and one trailing newline is trimmed.
File Required Content wg-private-key always the gateway’s base64 private key admin-token no bearer of the admin API and WebUI; without the file they are disabled provider--gateway-secret a go-authn provider the gateway client’s secret (was goauthn-gateway-secret, before v0.14.0) provider--secret each github provider the client secret of that provider’s GitHub OAuth app (see github_client_id; was github-client-secret, before v0.14.0) github-token when any tenant has members bearer for GET /users/{login} (see Tenants) A missing required file stops the start and names the file. Before reading, the server checks each file through its open descriptor (O_NOFOLLOW, then fstat) and refuses a symbolic link, anything but a regular file, a file readable by group or other, a file not owned by the server’s uid, an empty file and one over 64 KiB. One exception since v0.7.1: a file owned by uid 0 with mode exactly 0440 is accepted when its group is the server’s gid or one of its supplementary groups (what a Kubernetes Secret volume with fsGroup produces). A second one since v0.9.0, for systemd with DynamicUser=yes: systemd leaves the file root:root, mode 0400, plus a read-only POSIX ACL entry for the service’s uid (src/core/exec-credential.c:338-361, src/shared/acl-util.c:448-494), so stat shows 0440. The server reads system.posix_acl_access from the open descriptor and accepts exactly user:: (no write or execute), user::r--, group::---, mask::r--, other::---; any other named user or group, any write or execute bit, or a malformed or oversized value is refused. The error gives the fix.
Platform CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY Owner and mode systemd set by LoadCredentialEncrypted= with DynamicUser=yes (as shipped): root-owned with a read-only ACL for the service’s uid, accepted; with a fixed User= on a filesystem without ACLs: the service user, 0400. Private tmpfs Docker Swarm /run/secrets, set by hand mode: 0400 on the secret Docker Compose /run/secrets, set by hand the host file’s: chown and chmod 0400 it, and set user: to match Podman /run/secrets, set by hand --secret ...,mode=0400 (Quadlet: Secret=...,mode=0400) Kubernetes the Secret volume’s mount path, set by hand defaultMode: 0440 and fsGroup: the files are root:, accepted by the group rule above, so the pod runs as a non-root uid with every capability dropped but NET_ADMIN. add: [NET_ADMIN] alone does not give a non-root uid the capability (no ambient set): the image’s binary needs setcap cap_net_admin=+ep (per capabilities(7), not measured on a cluster) s6 (no systemd) /run/sdcreds/claimward-server, set by sdcreds s6-run the service user, 0400, in a private tmpfs (see s6) otherwise any directory chmod 0400, owned by the service user Ready-made units for systemd, Compose, Podman, Kubernetes and s6 are in the repository’s deploy/ directory, with the systemd-creds encrypt steps. Hosts without systemd get the same directory from go-authn/sdcreds (see s6); the server does not depend on it.
The organisation check of the github provider does not use github-token: it runs with the person’s token, so a private membership is visible only if that token carries read:org. The credential is optional while only organisations are used.
Migrating from v0.5.0 (breaking). ADMIN_TOKEN, WG_PRIVATE_KEY, WG_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_SECRET_FILE are no longer read, and the server refuses to start while one of them is set, naming the file to create. Put each value in its file (admin-token, wg-private-key, goauthn-gateway-secret), unset the variable and set CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY. A tenant with members now also needs github-token.
data.enrollment-rules#Enrollment rules: A key belongs to whoever enrolled it. Enrolling a key another identity holds is refused (409 key_taken): a public key is public, and taking one over would give the power to deregister its owner’s device. The same key enrolled again by its owner keeps its address and gets a new lease. The peer’s only allowed IP is the device’s /32, so devices cannot use each other’s addresses. The tenant is the one the caller asked for, if they are a member, or their only one. See Tenants.
data.how-it-programs-the-gateway#How it progr: The server uses wgctrl to add and remove peers on an existing interface, and checks at start-up that the interface exists. The interface itself (its private key and listen port) is left to wg-quick or systemd-networkd at boot, which keeps the privileged interface setup out of the long-running service.
data.openbsd#OpenBSD (pf):
From v0.10.0 the server also runs on OpenBSD, where it enforces the access policy with pf instead of nftables. It talks to the kernel directly through the /dev/pf ioctls; it never runs pfctl, and there is no pfctl fallback.
Supported releases: OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0. They share one struct pf_rule layout, which the server checks against the running release. On any other release the server refuses to start rather than risk encoding a rule wrongly.
You own pf.conf. The server never edits the main ruleset. Add one line to /etc/pf.conf and keep pf enabled:
anchor "claimward" The server loads the policy into that anchor. At start it reads the main ruleset back and verifies that it calls anchor "claimward".
It refuses to start when /dev/pf cannot be opened read-write (it must start as root), when pf is disabled, when the main ruleset does not call the anchor (the policy would be loaded and filter nothing), and when pf.conf has set skip on for the WireGuard interface (wg0, wg*), because pf would then never see the peers’ traffic.
Same policy as on Linux. Default deny on traffic arriving on WG_INTERFACE; only IPv4 is allowed, and IPv6 across the tunnel is dropped. The MSS clamp (TUNNEL_MTU) covers both families, as a match ... scrub (max-mss N) rule.
Atomic and fail closed. The anchor and its tables are replaced in one pf transaction, then read back and compared with what was meant to be loaded. If that fails, deny-all is loaded. The anchor stays in place when the process exits. Table names carry a per-load generation suffix, so that the short window between the table commit and the rule commit can never apply one tenant’s rules to another tenant’s peers.
Privilege separation (from v0.11.0). The pf promise of pledge(2) lets a process issue only twelve of the DIOC* ioctls (sys/kern/kern_pledge.c, pledge_ioctl), and the server also needs DIOCRINADEFINE, DIOCXROLLBACK, DIOCGETRULES, DIOCGETRULE, DIOCXEND and DIOCRGETADDRS; any other ioctl would kill the process. So the root parent, which drives /dev/pf, is not pledged. The unprivileged _claimward child, which holds the secrets and serves the network, is restricted with unveil(2) and pledge(2) before it serves (see below).
WireGuard peers (from v0.11.0). Before v0.11.0 an enrolment on OpenBSD failed when it added the peer to wg(4) (issue #79). The server now writes peers with the SIOCSWG and SIOCGWG ioctls of sys/net/if_wg.h and reads them back with its own decoder. Verified in real OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0 amd64 virtual machines: the structure layout matches the C compiler’s, and add, replace, remove and sweep work on a real wg(4) interface. OpenBSD on arm64 is only cross-compiled, not run on a kernel.
From v0.10.1 the repository ships deploy/openbsd/: an rc.d(8) script, an environment.example, a hostname.wg0.example and a pf.conf.example.
Two processes (from v0.11.0). The WireGuard peer configuration of wg(4) is behind suser(9) (sys/net/if_wg.c), and /dev/pf is guarded only by its device node, which is root-only: pfopen (sys/net/pf_ioctl.c) checks nothing else. OpenBSD has no privileged group that would let an unprivileged user do either, so the script starts the daemon as root (daemon_user="root") and the daemon splits in two. The parent (root) adds and removes peers, sets the tunnel MTU and loads the pf anchor; it reads no credential, serves no network and unveil(2)s only /dev/pf. The child, run as the _claimward user, holds the secrets, the TLS and gRPC listeners, the identity provider and the tenant policy, and is restricted with unveil(2) and pledge(2) (stdio rpath inet dns) before it serves. If it cannot drop privileges, the server does not start. The child asks the parent through a socketpair, and the parent refuses anything outside the address pool (VPN_CIDR). The _claimward user must exist and the ports must be above 1024 (the defaults 8443 and 8444 are); to serve on 443, redirect it with a pf rdr-to. Secrets are files in /etc/claimward/credentials, a 0700 directory owned by _claimward, with each file 0400 and owned by _claimward (install(1)). The script sets CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY to it; no secret goes in the environment, in arguments or in a URL. The non-secret settings are in /etc/claimward/environment, which stays root’s. wg0 must exist before the server starts: hostname.wg0 carries the same private key as the wg-private-key credential (mode 0640). install -m 0555 claimward-server /usr/local/bin/claimward-server useradd -g =uid -c claimward -d /var/empty -s /sbin/nologin -r 1..999 _claimward install -d -m 0755 -o root -g wheel /etc/claimward install -d -m 0700 -o _claimward -g _claimward /etc/claimward/credentials install -m 0400 -o _claimward -g _claimward wg-private-key /etc/claimward/credentials/wg-private-key install -m 0600 -o root -g wheel environment.example /etc/claimward/environment # then edit install -m 0640 -o root -g wheel hostname.wg0.example /etc/hostname.wg0 # then edit sh /etc/netstart wg0 install -m 0555 claimward_server /etc/rc.d/claimward_server rcctl enable claimward_server rcctl start claimward_server && rcctl check claimward_server rcctl start reports (ok) only once the server accepts connections on LISTEN_ADDR; a daemon that exits first, for instance on a credential the _claimward account does not own, is (failed).
The log goes to syslog (/var/log/daemon). The CI runs this script in real OpenBSD 7.9 and 8.0 virtual machines: rcctl start, the startup line, rcctl check, a root parent with one _claimward child, an enrolment through the child whose peer appears on wg0, and rcctl stop; then a start with a credential owned by root, and a start without the anchor in pf.conf, which must both fail.
data.providers#Identity providers:
Since v0.14.0 the server accepts several identity providers at once. They are listed in the JSON file named by PROVIDERS_FILE (unknown fields are refused, 1 MiB at most):
{"providers":[ {"id":"campus","kind":"oidc","name":"Campus","oidc_issuer":"https://idp.example.org","oidc_client_id":"claimward"}, {"id":"hub","kind":"github","name":"GitHub","github_client_id":"Iv1.0123456789abcdef","allowed_orgs":["my-org"]} ]} kind Fields besides id, kind, name Secret file github github_client_id, api_url (GitHub Enterprise), allowed_orgs provider--secret oidc oidc_issuer, oidc_client_id, allowed_domains none go-authn oidc_issuer, oidc_client_id, gateway_client_id provider--gateway-secret github: the bearer is a GitHub OAuth access token from the device flow. The server asks GitHub (Check a token) with the provider’s secret before trusting it, so only tokens that OAuth app minted are admitted, then resolves it through the GitHub API (/user, /user/orgs) and admits an active member of one of allowed_orgs, or a named tenant member (the list is optional only when a tenant has members). No client ID, no secret file, or neither an allowlist nor named members: the server refuses to start, with no opt-out. oidc: the bearer is an OIDC ID token, verified against the issuer with the audience oidc_client_id and the optional allowed_domains (the token’s email must be verified). go-authn: the bearer is an access token (at+jwt) from a go-authn/bridge provider, and the device’s key must be registered there by the same person. The server reads the provider’s signed list of registered keys (go-authn/wireguard) and drops from wg0 a key the provider takes back. At most one provider is of this kind. The request names its provider. Every API call carries the header Claimward-Provider: (gRPC: the metadata claimward-provider), and its token is judged by that provider alone: a token of provider A is refused when the request names B. No header is 401 missing_provider, an id the server does not list is 401 unknown_provider. The discovery document lists the providers (never a secret), so a client needs only the server’s URL.
One identity per issuer and sub. The identity is issuer#sub for oidc and go-authn, and github: for github: the same sub at two issuers is two people, and the second cannot take over the first’s device.
Tenants. A tenant gains a providers field, and its groups are written :. With several providers, a tenant that uses domains or idps must name providers, or the server fails closed.
Upgrading to v0.14.0 (breaking). AUTH_PROVIDER, OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID are no longer read, and the server refuses to start while one is set, naming the file that replaces it. Write the providers file, rename github-client-secret to provider--secret and goauthn-gateway-secret to provider--gateway-secret, write tenant groups as :, and expect a new subject for every person (issuer#sub, github:), so devices enrol again. Use client v0.9.0 or later: older clients do not send the header. See Identity providers for each flow end to end.
data.run-locally#Run locally:
With WG_DRYRUN=true no WireGuard device is touched:
cat > providers.json <<'EOF' {"providers":[{"id":"google","kind":"oidc","name":"Google","oidc_issuer":"https://accounts.google.com","oidc_client_id":"xxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com"}]} EOF export PROVIDERS_FILE=$PWD/providers.json export WG_ENDPOINT=vpn.example.com:51820 export CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY=$HOME/.local/state/claimward-dev-creds (umask 077; mkdir -p "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY"; wg genkey > "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/wg-private-key") chmod 0400 "$CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/wg-private-key" export WG_DRYRUN=true LISTEN_ADDR=:8080 go run ./cmd/claimward-server task run:dev does the same with GitHub sign-in and an ephemeral key, and task dex runs a local Dex to sign in against (deploy/dev/).
Run behind TLS. Bearer tokens are credentials: always serve the API over HTTPS, either with TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY or behind a TLS-terminating proxy, and give the RouteService a certificate so that devices get live route updates.
data.s6-deploy#Deploying under s6 (sdcreds):
From v0.10.2 the repository ships deploy/s6/claimward-server/ (run and finish) for hosts without systemd. sdcreds s6-run (go-authn/sdcreds v0.2.0 or later) decrypts every file of its --source directory into a private tmpfs, writes each one 0400 and owned by --user, sets CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, and starts the server as that user. A file owned by the process’s own uid with no group or other access is the first shape the loader accepts, so the loader is unchanged. Nothing secret goes in the environment, in argv or in a URL.
One capability, kept on purpose. The server needs CAP_NET_ADMIN (wgctrl, nftables, the interface MTU). s6-run empties every capability set of the service by default and keeps no_new_privs; the example passes --keep-cap=CAP_NET_ADMIN, so the server runs with exactly that one (CapEff 0x1000). The capability acts on the network namespace the supervision tree runs in: the host’s, unless you start s6-svscan inside one of its own (ip netns exec). Names. Each file of --source is named like its credential (wg-private-key, github-token, admin-token, provider--secret, provider--gateway-secret) and encrypted with sdcreds encrypt --name=; any other name stops the start. s6-run needs root and CAP_SYS_ADMIN (it mounts). Configuration that is not secret goes in /etc/claimward/env, read by the run script. Containers do not need it: Compose, Podman and Kubernetes mount secrets as files already (table above). The CI runs this directory under a real s6-svscan, in a network namespace with a real WireGuard link and nftables (not a dry run). It checks that the log holds the public key derived from the encrypted credential (and not a control key), that the server runs as the service user with CapEff 0x1000 and no_new_privs, that no secret is in its environment, that a credential file with mode 0644 is refused, and that stopping the service removes the mount.
data.what-it-serves#What it serves:
Listener Path Purpose LISTEN_ADDR (:8443) POST /api/v1/enroll verify, choose the tenant, allocate an address, add the peer, return the tunnel configuration GET /api/v1/tenants the tenants the caller may connect to POST /api/v1/heartbeat renew the device’s lease POST /api/v1/deregister remove the peer GET /healthz liveness GET /.well-known/claimward-configuration public discovery document, unauthenticated (since v0.13.0), see the protocol GET /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg the server’s logo, unauthenticated, only when SERVER_LOGO_FILE is set (since v0.14.0), see the protocol /admin/ admin API and WebUI, when the admin-token credential exists GRPC_ADDR (:8444) claimward.routes.v1.RouteService/Watch streams the tenant’s routes and their updates METRICS_ADDR (no default: off unless set) GET /metrics Prometheus metrics, on a listener of their own, never on LISTEN_ADDR The API requests carry Authorization: Bearer : a GitHub access token, an OIDC ID token, or a go-authn access token, depending on the provider they name in the Claimward-Provider header (since v0.14.0, see Identity providers). See the enrollment protocol for the payloads.
With TLS_CERT and TLS_KEY both listeners use TLS. Without them the HTTP API is plain (terminate TLS at a proxy), and so is the RouteService, which the clients then refuse except on loopback: devices connect, but get no live route updates.

data: claimward-vpn-app-windows v0.8.0 is a desktop app with a notification-area (tray) icon. Everything is Go with CGO_ENABLED=0: the window and the tray are drawn by go-widgets (no webview, no HTTP server in the app), except the four settings text fields, which are native Win32 Edit controls (system input method editors, selection, clipboard; they show no placeholder text), and the tunnel is wireguard-go on a Wintun adapter, configured through the IP Helper API. Its logic and helper are the shared pkg/appcore and pkg/helper.
data.configure#Configure:
The app reads %AppData%\Claimward\config.json, then CLAIMWARD_* variables (see the client library). The session is sealed with DPAPI in a per-user file, session.dpapi, under %AppData%\claimward. It is never written in clear and there is no plaintext fallback: if DPAPI fails (client v0.5.0 and later), sign-in fails with an error saying so. A session.json from an older version is moved into DPAPI on first start, or deleted if that fails.
The tunnel MTU is the server’s mtu, lowered to fit the path to the server (the interface MTU towards its endpoint, minus 60 for IPv4 or 80 for IPv6) and never below 1280 (client v0.6.0, pkg/pathmtu).
The helper reads C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.json:
{ "servers": ["https://vpn.example.org"], "group": "Claimward Users", "socket": "C:\\ProgramData\\Claimward\\helper.sock" } The service logs to C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.log; from an elevated console, claimward-helper run runs it in the foreground. The ACLs the helper sets and checks are described under Privileged helper.
Still to come: an MSI installer.
data.design#Design:
claimward-app.exe (the person, unprivileged) ├─ internal/ui/view.go widgets, bound by go-widgets/mvvmtk to … ├─ internal/ui/viewmodel.go … the ViewModel: all state, observables and commands ├─ internal/ui/tray_binding the tray menu, bound to the same ViewModel └─ appcore sign-in, session, tenant, helper client │ AF_UNIX socket, one JSON request each: C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.sock ▼ claimward-helper.exe — the ClaimwardHelper service (LocalSystem) pkg/helper enrolls with a server helper.json names, owns the tunnel pkg/wgtun wireguard-go on the Wintun adapter "Claimward"; address, routes, DNS, MTU The window shows the connection, the address and interface, who is signed in, the tenant and whether the helper answers; the device-flow prompt with a button that opens the page in the default browser (only an https page is ever handed to the shell); Connect / Disconnect / Sign out; Choose tenant; the settings, saved to %AppData%\Claimward\config.json; and the connection log. The status is polled every 2 seconds, by the shared pkg/appvm of the client (v0.7.0), which also decides what each button may do. When the tunnel drops, or the session expires, the app sends a notification once per change; clicking it opens the window (your own Disconnect is not announced). The tray menu offers the status, Connect, Disconnect, Open and Quit. Closing the window quits the app; the tunnel belongs to the service and stays up until Disconnect.
The tray icon appears from v0.3.0. Before it, the tray library had no Windows implementation of the call the app makes, and the app ignored the error, so v0.1.0 and v0.2.0 showed no tray icon. v0.3.0 is built with the tray library that implements it (go-widgets/tray v0.14.0). That is checked by compilation and the library’s own tests, not yet on a Windows desktop. Two known gaps: an icon that cannot be added is reported on stderr, which a windowed build does not show (#6), and quitting may leave a ghost icon until the pointer passes over it (go-widgets/tray#37).
data.install#Install:
From a release folder (scripts/package.sh builds them, with Wintun), in an elevated PowerShell:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass .\install.ps1 -Server https://vpn.example.org # optionally, the app's settings for the current user as well: .\install.ps1 -Server https://vpn.example.org -Provider github -GitHubClientId Iv1.0123456789abcdef It copies the programs and wintun.dll to C:\Program Files\Claimward, creates the local group Claimward Users and adds you to it, writes C:\ProgramData\Claimward\helper.json (after checking that directory, see below), registers and starts the ClaimwardHelper service, and adds a Claimward VPN Start Menu shortcut. Membership takes effect at your next sign-in to Windows; until then the socket refuses you. Add other people with Add-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Claimward Users' -Member .
-Server accepts https URLs only: the sign-in token is sent to that server.
ProgramData lets every user create directories, so the installer refuses a pre-existing C:\ProgramData\Claimward that is a reparse point (a link) or that is not owned by SYSTEM (S-1-5-18) or Administrators (S-1-5-32-544): inspect and remove it, then run the installer again.
.\uninstall.ps1 removes the service, the shortcut and the programs; -RemoveData also removes C:\ProgramData\Claimward and the group. There is no MSI yet.
package.sh downloads wintun-0.14.1.zip from wintun.net and refuses it unless its SHA-256 matches the one pinned in the script; the DLL is signed by WireGuard LLC and is not in the repository.

data: This walks through standing up a gateway and connecting a first device. The gateway is a Linux host; the device runs one of the three desktop apps.
Create the wg0 interface with a server key and a listen port. Claimward manages the peers of this interface; it does not create the interface.
# /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf [Interface] Address = 10.80.0.1/24 ListenPort = 51820 PrivateKey = wg genkey | tee server.key | wg pubkey > server.pub sudo wg-quick up wg0 sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 # if you route beyond the VPN subnet
data.2-run-the-control-plane#2. Run the contr: go install github.com/claimward/claimward-vpn-server/cmd/claimward-server@v0.14.0 export AUTH_PROVIDER=github # the default export GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS=claimward # an org allowlist, or name tenant `members` instead (the server refuses to start with neither) export WG_ENDPOINT=vpn.example.com:51820 export CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY=/etc/claimward/credentials # holds the file wg-private-key (0400, owned by the service user) export VPN_CIDR=10.80.0.0/24 export TLS_CERT=/etc/claimward/fullchain.pem # HTTPS, and TLS on the gRPC RouteService export TLS_KEY=/etc/claimward/privkey.pem export GRPC_ENDPOINT=vpn.example.com:8444 # where clients watch for route updates sudo -E "$(go env GOPATH)/bin/claimward-server" On Linux the server needs the rights to configure wg0 (root, or CAP_NET_ADMIN); for OpenBSD see OpenBSD. It listens on :8443 (LISTEN_ADDR) for the enrollment API and on :8444 (GRPC_ADDR) for the RouteService. See the server reference for every variable; for experiments without a real interface, set WG_DRYRUN=true.
data.3-register-the-sign-in-client#3. Registe: GitHub (default)OpenID Connectgo-authn Create a GitHub OAuth App (organisation or personal) and enable Device Flow in its settings. The apps need only its client ID, no secret. They ask for the scopes read:user, user:email and read:org.In your identity provider, create a native/public client with PKCE and the loopback redirect http://127.0.0.1:/callback. The port is picked at each sign-in, so the provider must accept any loopback port (RFC 8252). No client secret. Run the server with AUTH_PROVIDER=oidc, OIDC_ISSUER and OIDC_CLIENT_ID.At a go-authn/bridge provider, declare two clients: the one people sign in with (device = true, wireguard_keys = true, a refresh_lifetime), and the gateway’s own client (wireguard_peers). Run the server with AUTH_PROVIDER=go-authn. See Identity providers.
data.4-connect-a-device#4. Connect a device:
Each app has a privileged helper that enrolls with the server and owns the tunnel; it is installed once, as an administrator, with the servers it may connect to. The app itself runs as you.
macOSLinuxWindows From a checkout of claimward-vpn-app-osx:
sudo ./scripts/install-helper.sh https://vpn.example.com # the root LaunchDaemon task start:bundle # build Claimward.app and open it Then fill in the server URL, the provider and its client ID in Configuration… (or in ~/Library/Application Support/Claimward/config.json), and click Connect. See the macOS app.
From a checkout of claimward-vpn-app-linux:
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o bin/ ./cmd/... sudo ./scripts/install.sh --server https://vpn.example.com Log out and back in (the installer adds you to the claimward group), start Claimward VPN from your desktop’s menu, fill in the settings and click Connect. See the Linux app.
From a release folder built by scripts/package.sh of claimward-vpn-app-windows, in an elevated PowerShell:
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process Bypass .\install.ps1 -Server https://vpn.example.com -Provider github -GitHubClientId Iv1.0123456789abcdef Sign out of Windows and back in (the installer adds you to the Claimward Users group), start Claimward VPN from the Start Menu and click Connect. See the Windows app.
A person who belongs to several tenants is asked to choose one before the connection is made; see Tenants.
The device now has a tunnel interface (utunN on macOS, utun on Linux, the Wintun adapter Claimward on Windows) with its 10.80.0.x/32 address, and routes to the tenant’s networks through it.
Lease renewal comes with claimward-vpn-client v0.3.1, in the apps from v0.2.0: from then on the helper renews the lease while the tunnel is up and deregisters on Disconnect. The v0.1.0 apps do not: a connection that stays up longer than LEASE_TTL (24 hours by default) is removed from the gateway, and connecting again starts a new lease. See Leases.

data: Since server v0.14.0 (breaking) the server accepts several identity providers at once, listed in a JSON file named by PROVIDERS_FILE. The old single-provider variables (AUTH_PROVIDER, OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS, GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID) are no longer read, and the server refuses to start while one of them is set. The bearer the app obtains is opaque on the wire; how the server verifies it depends on the provider.
data.adding-a-provider#Adding a provider: On the server, implement Verifier (internal/auth) and register it in auth.New. On the client, implement Provider (pkg/auth) and register it in auth.New; a provider that keeps the devices’ keys itself also implements KeyRegistrar.
data.configuration#Configuration:
On the server, in PROVIDERS_FILE:
{"providers":[ {"id":"renater","kind":"go-authn","name":"RENATER", "oidc_issuer":"https://login.example.org", "oidc_client_id":"claimward", "gateway_client_id":"claimward-gw"} ]} oidc_client_id is the audience of the access tokens, gateway_client_id the gateway’s own client. The environment adds the credentials directory, which holds wg-private-key and provider-renater-gateway-secret (the gateway’s secret, a file only), and optionally the Shared Signals stream:
PROVIDERS_FILE=/etc/claimward/providers.json CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY=/etc/claimward/credentials GOAUTHN_SSF=true # optional At the provider (go-authn/bridge’s configuration):
wireguard { lifetime = "24h" # a key is listed this long; registering it again renews it max_keys = 10 # devices per person } client "claimward" { # the client people sign in with device = true wireguard_keys = true # its tokens, with the wireguard scope, may register a key refresh_lifetime = "720h" } client "claimward-gw" { # the gateway's own client secret_file = "/etc/bridge/claimward-gw.secret" wireguard_peers = ["claimward"] # it reads the keys registered through these clients ssf_receiver = true # optional: told at once when somebody is disabled } The client (v0.10.0 or later) reads the providers from the server’s discovery document, so its config.json needs only the server’s URL, and it sends the chosen provider’s id in Claimward-Provider:
{ "version": 2, "servers": [ {"url": "https://vpn.example.com"} ] } (provider may be added to an entry to remember the chosen provider’s id.)
data.go-authn#go-authn:
go-authn/bridge is an OpenID Connect provider in front of a SAML federation (RENATER, eduGAIN). It also keeps whose each WireGuard key is, so a valid token is no longer enough to enroll a device. At most one provider of the file is of this kind.
The app signs in with the provider’s device flow, scope openid wireguard. That token opens the provider’s key registry and nothing else: the provider addresses a token carrying one of its own scopes to itself alone. At every connection the app registers the device’s public key (POST /wireguard/key), which renews it when it is already the person’s, then refreshes for scope=openid alone. That gives an access token addressed to the VPN server. The provider rotates refresh tokens, and the app keeps the new one. The private key never leaves the device. The server accepts only an access token (typ: at+jwt, RFC 9068) whose audience is the provider’s oidc_client_id, never an ID token. It enrolls the key only if the provider’s list has it registered by the same subject; otherwise it answers 403 key_not_registered. A lease never outlives the key’s registration. The list comes from go-authn/wireguard:
it is fetched with the gateway’s own client (gateway_client_id, client_credentials, scope wireguard_peers, its secret in provider--gateway-secret) and signed by the provider for that gateway alone (typ: wireguard-peers+jwt); it is fetched again every GOAUTHN_PEER_LIST_INTERVAL (30 seconds by default). A key the provider takes back (the person or their institution disabled, or the device removed) is dropped from wg0 at the next fetch, and its heartbeat is refused; a list older than one already seen is refused, which is the replay protection; it fails closed: a list is valid five minutes, and past that the gateway admits nobody new, while tunnels already up end with their leases; the first list is fetched before the server listens: a gateway that cannot read it does not start; with GOAUTHN_SSF=true, the gateway also polls the provider’s Shared Signals stream (SSF 1.0, poll delivery, RFC 8936) every GOAUTHN_SSF_INTERVAL. An event only makes the list be fetched at once: it is a trigger, never a decision, so a forged event buys one extra fetch and nothing else. Tenants are matched on the token’s groups (eduPerson entitlements) and idp (the entity ID of the institution that vouched), and on the email’s domain only when the provider verified the address.
data.the-providers-file#The providers file:
PROVIDERS_FILE is a JSON object with a providers list. Unknown fields are refused, and the file is 1 MiB at most:
{"providers":[ {"id":"campus","kind":"oidc","name":"Campus","oidc_issuer":"https://idp.example.org","oidc_client_id":"claimward","allowed_domains":["example.org"]}, {"id":"hub","kind":"github","name":"GitHub","github_client_id":"Iv1.0123456789abcdef","allowed_orgs":["my-org"]}, {"id":"renater","kind":"go-authn","name":"RENATER","oidc_issuer":"https://login.example.org","oidc_client_id":"claimward","gateway_client_id":"claimward-gw"} ]} Every provider has an id (what a request names it by), a kind and a name (shown to the person). The other fields depend on the kind:
kind Sign-in on the device Bearer sent to the server Fields besides id, kind, name Secret file github OAuth device flow GitHub OAuth access token github_client_id, api_url (GitHub Enterprise), allowed_orgs provider--secret oidc authorization code + PKCE, in the browser OIDC ID token oidc_issuer, oidc_client_id, allowed_domains none go-authn device flow, then key registration go-authn access token (at+jwt) oidc_issuer, oidc_client_id, gateway_client_id provider--gateway-secret The secret files are credentials, files in CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, never variables (see Credentials). They were github-client-secret and goauthn-gateway-secret before v0.14.0.
The request names its provider. Every API call carries the header Claimward-Provider: (gRPC: the metadata claimward-provider), and its token is verified by that provider alone: a token of provider A is refused when the request names B. No header is 401 missing_provider, an id the server does not list is 401 unknown_provider. The discovery document (version 2) lists the providers, with no secret, so a client needs only the server’s URL.
One identity per issuer and sub. The identity is issuer#sub for oidc and go-authn, and github: for github: the same sub at two issuers is two people, and the second cannot take over the first’s device.
Tenants. A tenant gains a providers field, and its groups are written :. With several providers, a tenant that uses domains or idps must name providers, or the server fails closed. See tenants.
Logo. SERVER_LOGO_FILE (an SVG, 64 KiB at most, validated at start) is served at /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg, and the discovery document gives its path and sha256 under logo.

data.admin-api-and-webui#Admin API and WebUI:
With the admin-token credential present (a file in CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, see Credentials), the server serves an embedded Svelte WebUI at /admin/ and an API under /admin/api/, guarded by Authorization: Bearer (compared in constant time). Without the file, /admin/ answers 503. The WebUI’s files are served without authentication; it asks for the token and sends it with each call.
Method & path GET /admin/api/overview {"tenants", "peers", "watchers"} counts GET /admin/api/tenants every tenant POST /admin/api/tenants create one: id (or a slug of name), name, domains, groups, idps, members (logins; pinned is read-only, 400 if a login does not resolve), allowed_ips, dns GET /admin/api/tenants/{id} one tenant PUT /admin/api/tenants/{id} replace its name, membership lists and routes; bumps serial and pushes the routes to its watchers DELETE /admin/api/tenants/{id} delete it (not default); ends its watches Serve /admin/ only where administrators reach it: the token is a static shared secret.
data.gateway#Gateway: Bring up wg0 with wg-quick or systemd-networkd at boot; Claimward only manages its peers. Run the server with the rights to configure the interface and the firewall: on Linux root or CAP_NET_ADMIN (nftables); on OpenBSD root, for /dev/pf (see OpenBSD). On Linux, enable net.ipv4.ip_forward, and NAT or firewall rules, if clients route beyond the VPN subnet. GET /healthz is the liveness probe.
data.identity-provider#Identity provider: Since v0.14.0 the server takes one or several providers from the JSON file named by PROVIDERS_FILE (required, 1 MiB at most). The old variables AUTH_PROVIDER, OIDC_ISSUER, OIDC_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS and GOAUTHN_GATEWAY_CLIENT_ID are refused at start. A github provider needs a GitHub OAuth App with Device Flow enabled, its client secret in the file provider--secret, and allowed_orgs to restrict access. An oidc provider needs a native/public PKCE client, and allowed_domains restricts it. A go-authn provider uses the gateway’s own client (gateway_client_id, secret in provider--gateway-secret): the provider then decides which keys may connect, and a gateway that cannot fetch its list admits nobody new. Every request names its provider in the Claimward-Provider header (401 missing_provider, 401 unknown_provider). SERVER_LOGO_FILE publishes a logo at /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg. After a change to the file, restart the server. See Identity providers.
data.leases#Leases:
LEASE_TTL (24 hours by default) balances security and churn. The reaper removes expired peers every minute, so revoked or offline devices drop off on their own. To revoke one now, deregister its peer, or remove it with wg set wg0 peer remove.
From claimward-vpn-client v0.3.1 (the apps from v0.2.0), the helper renews the lease while the tunnel is up, at half of what is left (between 30 seconds and 10 minutes), and deregisters on Disconnect. A shorter LEASE_TTL therefore costs more heartbeats, not dropped tunnels: a removal from a tenant, or a key the go-authn provider takes back, ends the tunnel at the next renewal (the server answers 403). A server that has forgotten a device (404) gets it enrolled again. See Leases.
The v0.1.0 apps renew only by connecting again, and leave the peer until its lease ends after Disconnect: with them, a device that stays connected longer than LEASE_TTL loses its tunnel when its peer is reaped.
data.metrics#Metrics:
GET /metrics serves Prometheus metrics, without authentication, on its own listener: METRICS_ADDR, which has no default, so there are no metrics unless you set it (never on the enrollment port). They name every tenant: keep that listener on loopback or a private network.
Metric claimward_enrollments_total{tenant} successful enrollments claimward_active_peers enrolled peers claimward_tenants configured tenants claimward_route_watchers active RouteService watches claimward_tenant_route_serial{tenant} each tenant’s route serial
data.state#State:
The server keeps the enrolled peers, the address pool and the tenants in memory. A restart forgets them:
