the tenants are back to default alone, from PUSH_ROUTES and DNS; from server v0.2.0, the peers a previous run left on wg0 are removed at startup: every peer whose only allowed IP is a /32 inside VPN_CIDR, the shape the server gives every peer. Any other peer (configured by hand, a site-to-site link) is left alone. Kept, those peers would be nobody’s: never reaped, never checked against the provider’s list, so a person disabled before the restart would keep a working tunnel. Devices find themselves unknown at their next lease renewal and enroll again (apps built on claimward-vpn-client v0.3.1); until then their tunnel carries nothing. The helper renews at most 10 minutes apart, so after a restart a device can be cut off for up to 10 minutes. Reconnecting brings it back at once. the v0.1.0 server leaves those peers on wg0: it never reaps them, and it may hand their addresses to new devices (WireGuard then routes the address to the new peer). After restarting it, flush the peers (wg-quick down wg0 && wg-quick up wg0, or wg set … remove) and have devices connect again. For several gateways or a durable audit trail, the store, ipam and tenant packages need a database behind them.
data.tls#TLS:
The server speaks plain HTTP unless TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY are set. Bearer tokens are credentials, so always put the API behind TLS, directly or through a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, a load balancer).
The same certificate serves the gRPC RouteService. A route watch carries the bearer token, and the clients refuse a plaintext watch except on loopback: a server without TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY (for instance behind a proxy that only terminates HTTPS) enrolls devices, but they get no live route updates, and it logs a warning at start-up. Set GRPC_ENDPOINT to the host:port the devices reach the RouteService at, with a name the certificate covers.

data: Enrollment protocolThe HTTP API, its errors, and the gRPC RouteService.

The wire contract between the clients and the server. It is defined once in claimward-vpn-client/pkg/protocol (HTTP) and proto/routes/v1/routes.proto (gRPC), and imported by both sides.
Every authenticated request sends the person’s bearer as Authorization: Bearer , never in the body: a GitHub OAuth access token (a github provider), an OIDC ID token (oidc), or a go-authn access token (go-authn). Since server v0.14.0 the request also names the provider that issued it, in the header Claimward-Provider: (gRPC: the metadata claimward-provider), an id from the discovery document’s providers. The token is judged by that provider alone. No header is 401 missing_provider; an id the server does not list, or several ids, is 401 unknown_provider. Request bodies are JSON, at most 64 KiB, and unknown fields are refused.
data.discovery#GET /.well-known/claimward-con:
The public discovery document (since server v0.13.0), unauthenticated, so that a client can learn how to sign in before it does. The path follows RFC 8615 section 3; a claim without a value is omitted, as in RFC 8414 section 3.2. Public values only, never a secret. Response 200, application/json, Cache-Control: public, max-age=300; any other method is refused with 405.
{ "version": 2, "server_name": "Lab", "providers": [ { "id": "hub", "kind": "github", "name": "GitHub", "github_client_id": "Iv1.0123456789abcdef" }, { "id": "campus", "kind": "oidc", "name": "Campus", "oidc_issuer": "https://idp.example.org", "oidc_client_id": "claimward" } ], "exclusive": false, "logo": { "path": "/.well-known/claimward-logo.svg", "sha256": "" } } Version 2 (server v0.14.0, breaking) replaces the single provider and its fields of version 1 by the list providers, one entry per provider of PROVIDERS_FILE, in file order: id (what the client sends in Claimward-Provider), kind (github, oidc or go-authn), name (shown to the person), then github_client_id for github, oidc_issuer and oidc_client_id for oidc and go-authn. A client of version 0.10.0 or later reads it; it refuses a document of a version it does not know. server_name appears only when SERVER_NAME is set, logo only when SERVER_LOGO_FILE is. exclusive is SERVER_EXCLUSIVE: this server refuses to share the machine with other Claimward tunnels, clients refuse to connect it alongside others, and refuse others while it is connected.
data.errors#Errors:
Non-2xx responses carry:
{ "error": "invalid_token", "message": "…" } Code Status Meaning missing_token / invalid_token 401 no bearer, or the provider’s verification failed (including an organisation or domain allowlist) missing_provider 401 no Claimward-Provider header (since v0.14.0) unknown_provider 401 the header names a provider the server does not list, or several (since v0.14.0) bad_public_key / bad_request 400 malformed input key_not_registered 403 go-authn: the key is not registered at the provider by this person not_a_member 403 the tenant asked for is not one of the caller’s, or no longer is not_owner 403 deregister: the key belongs to another person not_enrolled 404 heartbeat: no enrollment of this key by the caller key_taken 409 enroll: the key is enrolled by another person tenant_required 409 enroll: the caller belongs to several tenants and named none; the message lists them pool_exhausted 503 no free address in VPN_CIDR gateway_error 500 the peer could not be added to WireGuard
data.get-apiv1tenants#GET /api/v1/tenants:
Response 200: the tenants the caller may connect to.
[ { "id": "default", "name": "Default" } ]
data.logo#GET /.well-known/claimward-logo.svg: The server’s logo (since server v0.14.0), unauthenticated, present only when SERVER_LOGO_FILE is set; otherwise 404. The discovery document’s logo gives its path and the sha256 (hex) of its bytes, so a client can cache it and notice a change. Response 200: Content-Type: image/svg+xml, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; sandbox, and ETag set to the same hash; a request with a matching If-None-Match gets 304. The server validates the file at start (at most 64 KiB, no script, no external reference, no DOCTYPE) and refuses to start on an invalid one. A client must still treat it as untrusted and render it as an image, never inline.
data.post-apiv1deregister#POST /api/v1/deregi: { "public_key": "" } Response 204, also for a key that is not enrolled. 403 not_owner if the key belongs to another person.
data.post-apiv1enroll#POST /api/v1/enroll:
Request:
{ "public_key": "", "device": { "name": "alice-mbp", "os": "darwin", "platform": "app-osx" }, "tenant": "hpc" } tenant is optional: without it the server uses the person’s only tenant. The helpers send os darwin, linux or windows and platform app-osx, app-linux or app-windows.
Response 200:
{ "assigned_ip": "10.80.0.5/32", "server_public_key": "", "endpoint": "vpn.example.com:51820", "allowed_ips": ["10.80.0.0/24"], "dns": ["10.80.0.1"], "grpc_endpoint": "vpn.example.com:8444", "persistent_keepalive": 25, "lease_expires_at": "2026-10-06T10:00:00Z" } allowed_ips and dns are the tenant’s. dns is left out when the tenant has none, grpc_endpoint when the server advertises no RouteService (GRPC_ENDPOINT). mtu is the tunnel MTU in bytes (an integer, 1280 to 9000), left out when the server has none to advertise. Since server v0.7.0 it is always set: TUNNEL_MTU, or the uplink MTU minus 80 (at most 1420). The client applies it, then lowers it to fit its own path (the interface MTU towards the endpoint minus 60 for IPv4, 80 for IPv6, never below 1280); it never raises it. Absent means 1420.
data.post-apiv1heartbeat#POST /api/v1/heartbe: { "public_key": "" } Response 200: { "lease_expires_at": "..." }. 404 not_enrolled if the key is not enrolled by the caller, 403 not_a_member once the person has left the session’s tenant, 403 key_not_registered (go-authn) once the provider no longer lists the key.
data.routeservice-grpc#RouteService (gRPC):
package claimward.routes.v1; service RouteService { rpc Watch(WatchRequest) returns (stream RouteUpdate); } message WatchRequest { string public_key = 1; } message RouteUpdate { repeated string allowed_ips = 1; repeated string dns = 2; uint64 serial = 3; // increases on each change } The server listens on GRPC_ADDR and advertises GRPC_ENDPOINT in the enrollment response. The bearer travels in the metadata, authorization: Bearer , with the provider in claimward-provider, and is verified as for the HTTP API (UNAUTHENTICATED when either is wrong). Watch sends the current set at once, then a new one each time the tenant’s routes change, for the tenant the device enrolled into, found by public_key, which must be enrolled by the caller (NOT_FOUND otherwise, PERMISSION_DENIED once the person has left that tenant).
The server serves it over TLS with TLS_CERT/TLS_KEY. The clients (pkg/routeclient) speak TLS to it, checked against the system’s roots, except to a loopback address, and refuse a plaintext one.

data:
The helper runs as root (SYSTEM on Windows) and a server it enrolls with chooses the routes and the peer of the machine’s tunnel: a hostile server is every packet of the machine, sent there. Since client v0.11.0 the helper takes a server from the app only if one of these holds:
the administrator’s configuration names it (servers in helper.json, now optional: the pre-approval); it was approved before, and still says what it said then; it is approved now, with the consent of the operating system, obtained by the helper itself. An app flag, a field of the request, or a claim of any kind is never consent.
data.errors-the-app-sees#Errors the app sees: Code Meaning server_not_approved the server is neither pre-approved nor approved: ask the person to approve it server_identity_changed it was approved, and no longer says the same: approve it again approval_denied the system’s consent was not given
data.limits-stated#Limits, stated: On macOS the text of the prompt is supplied by the app that asks, so a hostile process in the socket’s group can make the system ask an administrator to approve its own server, and a distracted administrator can say yes. The credential is an administrator’s, never cached, and good for one approval. On Windows, an elevated process can approve anything, as an administrator can edit the file anyway. Linux has no cache either: auth_admin asks every time.
data.what-is-asked-of-the-system#What is aske: Platform Consent macOS Authorization Services right com.claimward.helper.approve-server, rule authenticate-admin-nonshared: an administrator’s name and password, every time. The app obtains the authorization (macauth.Obtain) and sends its 32-byte external form; the helper has the system verify it and destroys it, so one token buys one approval. A forged token names nothing in the system and is refused Linux polkit action com.claimward.helper.approve-server (auth_admin), asked of the system bus for the process behind the socket: its pid from SO_PEERCRED and its start time from /proc//stat, which defeats pid reuse. The policy file ships in packaging/polkit/ and goes in /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/ Windows a second socket, C:\ProgramData\Claimward\approve.sock, whose ACL names SYSTEM and Administrators only: a standard user cannot connect without UAC elevation. Only a request that came in on it counts With no authorizer configured the helper refuses every approval: it fails closed. A request that is refused, or that the system cannot answer, changes nothing.
data.what-is-remembered#What is remembered:
The helper keeps the approved servers in a file only root can write:
Platform File macOS /var/db/claimward/approved-servers.json Linux /var/lib/claimward/approved-servers.json Windows C:\ProgramData\Claimward\approved-servers.json Each entry is the server’s canonical URL and the SHA-256 of its discovery identity: its name and its identity providers (id, kind, issuer, client ids). A server that changes one of those is not the one that was approved: the helper refuses it (server_identity_changed) until it is approved again. Whether the server is exclusive, its logo and the providers’ display names are not part of the identity, and neither is its TLS certificate, which is renewed every few weeks (the connection is verified against the web PKI at each use).
The file is read afresh at every use, so deleting it, or removing a line, revokes at once; the revoke action does the same for one server. An administrator’s servers list is never edited by the helper.

data: A tenant is a set of routes (allowed_ips) and DNS servers, and the rules that say who belongs to it. A person may belong to several tenants: they choose one per session, and the device connects to that one.
data.access-policy#Access policy:
A tenant’s routes are not only advertised: the gateway enforces them. A tenant may carry a policy, a list of rules that say which destination a peer may reach, on which protocol and ports:
[{"id": "default", "policy": [ {"cidr": "10.20.0.5/32", "proto": "tcp", "ports": [445, 88]}, {"cidr": "10.20.0.5/32", "proto": "udp", "ports": [88]} ]}] proto is tcp or udp; ports are numbers or ranges ("9000-9010"), and are required. IPv4 only. The allowed_ips pushed to the clients are derived from the policy (the distinct CIDRs), so what a device routes and what the gateway lets through cannot drift apart. The route format is unchanged. The gateway owns one nftables table, inet claimward, installed through netlink (Linux, CAP_NET_ADMIN), or on OpenBSD the pf anchor claimward loaded through /dev/pf (see OpenBSD). Either is replaced atomically at start and at every peer or tenant change. Traffic arriving from the WireGuard interface is denied by default, in both the forward chain and the input chain (the file server may be the gateway host itself); each peer’s address is matched against its tenant’s rules. DNS must be named in the policy like anything else. Fail closed: if the ruleset cannot be installed, the server does not start, and an enrollment whose ruleset cannot be installed is refused (500 gateway_error). A tenant with allowed_ips and no policy is enforced as any protocol, any port, to those CIDRs. Tenants with a policy are loaded at start from the JSON file named by TENANTS_FILE (an array of tenants with the admin API’s fields); the admin API accepts policy too. The admin WebUI does not edit it yet.
data.choosing-one-per-session#Choosing one pe:
Request What the server does GET /api/v1/tenants lists the tenants the caller may connect to, [{"id", "name"}], for a client to offer the choice POST /api/v1/enroll with tenant the tenant must be one of them, or 403 not_a_member POST /api/v1/enroll without tenant the caller’s only tenant; a person in several gets 409 tenant_required, with the list in the message, rather than being routed into a network they did not choose POST /api/v1/heartbeat refused with 403 not_a_member once the person is no longer in the session’s tenant RouteService Watch streams the routes of the tenant the device enrolled into, found by the device’s key, which must be the caller’s In the apps (pkg/appcore):
Tenants asks the server, through the helper, which tenants the person may join; SetTenant records the choice in the session, and only a tenant the server offered; a new sign-in forgets it; Connect enrolls into that tenant. A person in several who has not chosen gets ErrTenantRequired, with the tenants in the status. A person in one tenant never chooses. The macOS app opens its window when a Connect from the menu bar is refused for want of a choice; the Linux and Windows apps show the choice in their window. The Linux app does not let the tenant change while connected.
data.members#Named members:
members lists GitHub logins, readable but renameable: a login can be released and registered by somebody else. The server therefore pins each login to the account’s numeric ID. When a tenant is loaded (TENANTS_FILE) or created or updated through the admin API, it calls GET {GITHUB_API_URL}/users/{login} (10 s timeout, 64 KiB answer cap, the account must be a User) and stores the pair in the read-only pinned field. A person is a member when their token’s subject is github: for a pinned ID: a renamed account whose old login now belongs to somebody else is refused. An unresolvable login is an error: the server refuses to start, and the admin API answers 400. The admin API and WebUI show the logins; to follow a rename, edit the tenant again. Resolution is authenticated with the github-token credential (a file in CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY, sent as a bearer: 5000 requests an hour on github.com). A tenant with members and no github-token stops the start; the token is never sent over plain HTTP except to a loopback address.
A named member is also admitted by the GitHub entry gate without belonging to an allowed organisation (see identity providers).
data.membership#Membership:
A person belongs to every tenant that names any of:
Field Matched against domains the domain of a verified email address (an unverified one is a string the person typed) groups the token’s groups claim (OIDC; go-authn: eduPerson entitlements), or the person’s GitHub organisations idps the institution that vouched for them: go-authn’s idp, a SAML entity ID members GitHub logins, named one by one, pinned to the account’s numeric ID (below) A person who matches no tenant is refused (v0.5.0, breaking): 403 not_a_member on /api/v1/tenants and /api/v1/enroll, and the gRPC Watch is refused. There is no fallback tenant any more: the default tenant receives only those its own domains, groups, idps or members name. An unknown tenant ID is an error, never the default tenant’s routes. Migrating from v0.4.x. People who used to land in default must now be named by it: give the default entry of TENANTS_FILE the domains, groups, idps or members that name them, then restart. The default tenant created from PUSH_ROUTES and DNS alone names nobody.
data.route-updates#Route updates: Editing a tenant’s routes bumps its serial and pushes the new set to every device watching that tenant over the gRPC RouteService. The helper replaces the WireGuard peer’s allowed IPs and adds or removes the matching routes, without enrolling again. Deleting a tenant ends its watches.
data.where-tenants-come-from#Where tenants co:
The server starts with one tenant, default, whose routes are PUSH_ROUTES (by default VPN_CIDR) and whose DNS servers are DNS. Other tenants are created, edited and deleted through the admin API and WebUI, which edit the four membership lists beside the routes. The default tenant cannot be deleted.
Tenants are kept in memory (v0.2.0): a restart of the server leaves only the default tenant, rebuilt from the environment.
